steps.text: Toss the diced strawberries with the sugar and chopped dates in a small bowl. Set aside to macerate while you make the fritters; they will turn glossy and syrupy.
Put the grated taro in a clean tea towel or your hands and squeeze out as much liquid as you can. Tip it into a large bowl.

Add the honeycomb at the very end so it melts into a glaze instead of catching and burning.
Taste the sauce before adding any salt, as black bean sauce is already well seasoned.
Keep the onion rings on the top shelf of the oven so they stay crisp until serving.

steps.text: Put the wood ear mushroom in a bowl, cover with warm water and leave to soak for 20 minutes until soft and springy. Drain, rinse, trim off any hard knobbly bits and slice into strips.

While the mushroom soaks, heat the oven to 220C (200C fan). Spread the crinkle-cut chips on a tray, toss with a little cooking oil and bake for 25 to 30 minutes, turning once, until crisp and golden. Season with salt.
Season the opah chunks lightly with salt and black pepper. Set aside while you start the broth.
Warm the cooking oil in a wide, deep pan over a medium heat. Add the garlic and fry for 1 minute until fragrant and just turning pale gold, without letting it brown.
Add the blewit and sliced wood ear mushroom and cook for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring now and then, until the blewit softens and releases its juices.
Stir in the chopped kimchi with its juices and cook for 2 minutes to deepen the flavour.
Pour in the sparkling wine, scraping up anything stuck to the base of the pan. Let it bubble for 3 minutes to cook off the sharp edge of the alcohol, then add the water and bring to a gentle simmer.

Lower the heat so the broth barely trembles. Slide in the opah chunks and simmer gently for 6 to 8 minutes, until the fish is opaque and just cooked through. Avoid stirring too hard so the pieces stay whole.
Taste the broth and adjust with salt and black pepper. Ladle the opah, mushrooms, kimchi and broth into two warm bowls.
Pile the hot crinkle-cut chips on top of each bowl and serve straight away, so they stay crisp for dunking.

tips: Opah is firm and rich, so keep the simmer gentle to stop it turning dry.
Add the chips at the very last moment; they soften quickly in the hot broth.
If the broth tastes too sharp, simmer it for a few more minutes before adding the opah.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan) and grease a baking tray lightly with a little of the butter. Take the puff pastry out of the fridge so it is easy to unroll.

Warm the black beans in the soup over a low heat for 2 minutes, stirring now and then, so they heat through without breaking up.

tips: Never boil the soup once the cockles are in; gentle residual heat keeps them tender.
Use balsamic vinegar sparingly, just a few drops per bowl, so it lifts the sweetness without taking over.

Roughly chopped, with its juices kept
Base trimmed and strands gently separated
Woody ends snapped off, spears cut into 3cm pieces

steps.text: Rinse the green split peas in a sieve under cold water, then tip them into a medium saucepan with the dried bay leaf and 900ml of water.
Bring to the boil over a high heat, skimming off any foam that rises, then turn the heat down low so the pan barely bubbles.
Simmer gently, partly covered, for 40 minutes, stirring now and then, until the peas have collapsed and the soup is thick enough to coat a spoon. Add a splash of water if it becomes too thick.

Fish out the bay leaf. Stir in the chopped kimchi with its juices and half of the butter, then simmer for 5 minutes so the tang and gentle heat spread through the soup. Season with salt and black pepper.
Add the asparagus pieces and simmer for 3 minutes, until bright green and still crisp. Stir in the enoki for the final minute only, so it stays tender with a little bite. Turn off the heat.

While the soup finishes, bring a small pan of water to a very gentle simmer. Crack each free-range egg into a cup, slide it into the water and cook for 3 minutes, until the white is set and the yolk is still runny. Lift out with a slotted spoon and drain briefly.
Ladle the soup into two warm bowls and top each with a free-range egg. Add a grind of black pepper. Butter the cornbread with the remaining butter and serve alongside for dunking.

tips: Keep the heat low while the peas cook, because they catch easily on the bottom of the pan once they begin to thicken.
Taste before adding salt, as kimchi is already salty.
Break the yolk into the soup at the table so it enriches each spoonful, and dunk the buttered cornbread in the mixture.

steps.text: Slice the beef silverside as thinly as you can against the grain, then season with half the salt and the black pepper. Chop the kimchi and sauerkraut, and cut the guar beans into short lengths. Tear the spearmint leaves and set aside.

Bring the water to the boil in a large pan and salt it well. Cook the spaghetti for 9 to 10 minutes until just tender. Add the guar beans for the final 2 minutes so they blanch briefly. Reserve a mugful of the cooking water, then drain.
While the pasta cooks, cook the mozzarella sticks as directed on the pack until golden and crisp. Keep them warm.

Heat the cooking oil in a large frying pan over a high heat. Add half the butter and, once foaming, fry the beef in a single layer in two batches for about 1 to 2 minutes per batch until well browned. Lift out onto a plate.

Lower the heat to medium and add the remaining butter. Stir in the kimchi and sauerkraut and cook for 2 minutes until sizzling. Pour in the pickling vinegar and scrape up the browned bits from the base of the pan, letting it bubble for 30 seconds.

Return the beef and any juices to the pan, add the spaghetti and guar beans, and toss well, loosening with a splash of the reserved cooking water until glossy. Taste and adjust with salt and black pepper.
Divide between two warm bowls. Break the hot mozzarella sticks over the top and scatter with the torn spearmint. Serve straight away.

tips: Pat the beef dry before frying so it browns rather than steams.
Fry the beef in batches; crowding the pan will make it stew and turn grey.
Add the pickling vinegar a little at a time and taste, as kimchi and sauerkraut are already tangy.

steps.text: Soak the wood ear mushroom in a bowl of warm water for 20 minutes until soft and springy. Drain, trim off any hard knobs and slice into thin strips.
Heat the cooking oil in a medium saucepan over a medium heat. Add the sliced ginger and cook for 1 minute until fragrant, then add the octopus pieces and stir for 2 minutes.

Pour in 500ml water, add half the salt and half the black pepper, and bring to a gentle boil. Reduce the heat to low, cover and simmer for 50 to 60 minutes until the octopus is tender when pierced with a knife.
Stir the grated ginger, sliced wood ear mushroom and baby sweetcorn into the pan. Simmer, uncovered, for 8 minutes.

Meanwhile, put the couscous in a heatproof bowl with a pinch of salt. Pour over 300ml boiling water, cover with a plate and leave for 5 minutes, then fluff with a fork.
Divide the couscous between two warm bowls. Spoon over the octopus, vegetables and plenty of the gingery broth, then finish with a generous grinding of black pepper.

tips: If the octopus is still chewy after an hour, keep simmering gently and test every 10 minutes.
Keep the simmer very gentle; a hard boil will toughen the octopus.
Add the asparagus last so it stays green and snappy.

steps.text: Put the rinsed sushi rice in a small pan with 180ml water and a pinch of salt. Bring to the boil, cover, turn the heat very low and cook for 12 minutes. Take off the heat and leave covered for 10 minutes, then press the rice into two firm patties.

Roll the egg noodle dough out thinly on a floured-free, lightly oiled surface, using a little cooking oil to stop sticking. Fold and cut into ribbons about 1cm wide. Shake them loose and keep them covered while the water heats.

Bring a large pan of well-salted water to a rolling boil. Boil the noodle ribbons for 2 to 3 minutes until just tender, then drain, keeping a small cup of the cooking water. Toss the noodles with a splash of oil so they do not clump.

Heat a wide frying pan over a medium-high heat with 1 tbsp oil. Fry the chorizo for 4 to 5 minutes until crisp at the edges and the oil has turned red. Add the crushed juniper berries and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.

Wipe the small pan, heat the remaining oil and fry the rice patties for 2 to 3 minutes per side until golden and crisp. Pile the noodles into warm bowls and serve with the crisped sushi rice alongside.

tips: Crush the juniper berries as finely as you can, so every forkful carries a little resinous heat.
Do not overcook the noodles in the water, as they finish cooking in the hot pan with the chorizo oil.
Press the sushi rice patties firmly and leave them alone in the oil until they release easily, then turn once.

steps.text: Build a steady fire and let it burn down to glowing embers with a few small flames. Set your sturdiest pot on a grate or stones over the heat. Chop the kimchi, slice the beans, chop the almonds and peel the clementine into segments before the light fades.

Put the fish bones in the pot with the water and a pinch of salt. Bring to a gentle simmer, skimming off any grey scum. Simmer for 25 minutes, keeping the heat low, until the broth smells rich and tastes savoury.
Strain the broth through a sieve or clean cloth into a heatproof container, discarding the bones. Wipe out the pot, return it to the embers and keep the broth hot at the edge of the fire.
Melt half the butter in the pot over a medium heat. Add the rice and stir for 2 minutes until the grains turn glossy and smell lightly toasted.

Add a ladle of hot broth and stir until it is absorbed. Keep adding broth a ladle at a time, stirring often, moving the pot nearer or further from the flames to keep a lazy bubble. Continue for about 18 minutes.

Meanwhile, melt the remaining butter in a small pan or on a flat stone at the fire's edge. Add the almonds, toast for 2 minutes, then pour over the maple syrup and turn for 1 minute until glossy and sticky. Tip onto a plate to cool.

When the rice is nearly tender, stir in the chopped kimchi with its juices and the beans. Cook for 4 minutes more, adding broth as needed, until the beans are just tender and the rice is creamy and loose.
Take the pot off the heat and stir in most of the Manchego and the black pepper. Taste and add a little salt if needed. Rest for 1 minute.
Spoon the risotto into bowls straight from the pot. Top with the glazed almonds, the remaining Manchego and the clementine segments. Eat by the fire at dusk.

tips: Keep the pot moving closer to or further from the flames rather than fighting the fire; a gentle bubble gives the creamiest rice.
Taste the kimchi before adding salt, as it already brings plenty of seasoning.
Add the clementine at the very end so its fresh brightness stays sharp against the smoky rice.

steps.text: In a large bowl mix the plain flour, semolina, chestnut flour, yeast and 1/2 teaspoon salt. Add the lukewarm water and the softened butter, then stir to a soft, slightly sticky dough.
Knead on a lightly floured surface for about 8 minutes until smooth and elastic. Return to the bowl, cover and leave somewhere warm until nearly doubled in size.
Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan). Grease a large baking tray with a little butter and dust it with semolina.
Toss the thin sweet potato slices with a pinch of salt and a few grinds of black pepper. Spread them on a second tray and roast for 12 minutes until just tender and starting to colour at the edges.
Knock the air out of the dough and stretch or roll it into a round about 28cm across on the prepared tray. Prick the middle a few times with a fork and leave to rest for 10 minutes.
Scatter the chopped kimchi over the base, leaving a small border. Arrange the roasted sweet potato and whole baby button mushrooms on top, then lay the Camembert slices over the lot.
Bake on the hot oven shelf for 16 to 18 minutes until the edges are crisp and golden and the Camembert is molten and bubbling.
Grate the fresh ginger over the hot round, add a final grind of black pepper, then rest for 2 minutes before cutting into wedges.

tips: Pat the kimchi with the back of a spoon to drain it, so the base stays crisp rather than soggy.
Slice the sweet potato thinly and evenly so it softens in the pre-roast and then crisps at the edges in the bake.
Chestnut flour has no gluten, so keep it to a small amount and knead well for a springy dough.

Heat half the cooking oil in a frying pan over a high heat. Sear the lotus root rounds for 2 to 3 minutes each side until golden and lightly crisp at the edges. Lift out and keep warm.
Add the remaining cooking oil to the same pan and sear the sliced cep for 3 to 4 minutes until deeply browned on both sides. Season with a small pinch of salt.
Lift the pork from the broth onto a board and shred it with two forks. Return the shredded meat to the pan and taste the broth, adding a little more salt only if needed.
Bring the broth back to a steady boil. Drop in the strips of egg noodle dough and cook for 3 to 4 minutes until tender and slightly chewy.
Divide the noodles, shredded pork and broth between two warm bowls. Top with the seared cep, lotus root, guar beans and white kimchi, then finish with the chilli flakes.

tips: Keep the simmer very gentle; a hard boil toughens the pork and turns the broth cloudy.
Tamari is already salty, so hold back on extra salt until you have tasted the finished broth.
Sear the cep in a single layer without crowding so they brown rather than steam.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan). Take the lamb out of its packaging, pat it dry and leave it on the side while the oven heats.

Cut each bruised lemongrass stalk into 3 or 4 pieces. With a small sharp knife, make 8 to 10 deep slits all over the lamb. Push a whole garlic clove or a piece of lemongrass into each slit, using all 4 cloves and all the lemongrass.
Rub the lamb all over with 1 tablespoon of the vegetable oil, 1 teaspoon of salt and the black pepper.

Toss the sweet potato chunks in a large roasting tin with 1 tablespoon of the vegetable oil and a pinch of salt. Spread them out in a single layer, leaving a space in the middle, and set the lamb on top.
Roast for 30 minutes, until the lamb has started to colour and the sweet potato is just beginning to soften at the edges.
Meanwhile, stir the orange curd with the water until it is loose enough to brush. Rub the cabbage wedges with the remaining tablespoon of vegetable oil.
Take the tin out. Brush about half of the loosened orange curd over the lamb. Tuck the cabbage wedges around the sweet potato, cut side down, and turn the sweet potato in the juices.

Return the tin to the oven for 25 minutes. Brush the lamb with the rest of the orange curd halfway through, and turn the cabbage wedges once so they char at the edges. The lamb is ready for pink at 58C in the thickest part, or leave it 10 minutes longer for well done.
Lift the lamb onto a board, cover loosely with foil and rest for 15 minutes. Leave the vegetables in the switched-off oven to stay hot and finish crisping.

Pick out the lemongrass pieces, which are for flavour only. Slice the lamb thickly against the grain and arrange it over the sweet potato and cabbage. Spoon over the sticky juices from the tin, then scatter the pomegranate seeds over the top and serve straight away.

tips: Pat the lamb dry before rubbing it with oil, as this helps the outside brown and the glaze stick.
If the orange curd begins to darken too much, loosely cover the lamb with foil for the last 10 minutes.
Keep the pomegranate seeds for the very end so they stay juicy and bright rather than cooked.

Drop the egg noodles into the boiling water and cook for about 5 minutes until just tender. Drain well and set aside, tossing with a few drops of cooking oil so they do not clump.
Heat the pouch of microwave noodles following the packet instructions, usually about 1 to 2 minutes, then tip into a bowl and loosen with a fork.

Heat the remaining oil in the large frying pan over a high heat until shimmering. Season the pork with a pinch of salt and the black pepper, then fry the strips for 3 to 4 minutes, turning rarely, until browned at the edges.

Add the crushed garlic cloves and fry for 30 seconds until fragrant, then pour in the cooking wine. Let it bubble and reduce for about 1 minute, scraping up the sticky bits, until the pork is glossy and sticky.

Tip in the chopped kimchi with its juice and the sauerkraut and stir for 1 minute until hot and sizzling. Add both lots of noodles and the sugar snap peas, then toss everything over a high heat for 2 minutes so the peas stay crunchy and the noodles pick up the sticky juices.
Taste and add a little more salt or pepper if needed. Pile high into two paper trays or deep bowls and eat straight away, messy and hot, with a fork.

tips: Keep the pan very hot and do not crowd it, so the pork browns rather than steams.
Slice the pork against the grain as thinly as you can for quick, tender strips.
Add the sugar snap peas at the very end so they keep their snap.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan). Toss the sweet potato cubes with a little of the butter, melted, a pinch of salt and some black pepper. Spread on a baking tray in a single layer.
Roast the sweet potato for 25 minutes, turning once, until soft and lightly browned at the edges. Leave the oven on.
Meanwhile, bring the water to the boil in a large pan with a good pinch of salt. Cook the rigatoni for 2 minutes less than the packet says, so it is still firm. Drain and set aside.
Melt the remaining butter in a saucepan over a medium heat. Stir in the grated ginger and chilli powder and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the flour and stir for 1 to 2 minutes to make a paste. Pour in the milk a splash at a time, whisking well after each addition so there are no lumps.
Add the bouquet garni and simmer gently for 8 minutes, stirring often, until the gravy coats the back of a spoon. Season with salt and black pepper, then remove and discard the bouquet garni.
Fold the drained rigatoni, roasted sweet potato and drained tinned carrots into the gravy, taking care not to break up the carrots too much. Tip into a lightly buttered baking dish.
Bake for 15 minutes until bubbling at the edges. Dot the torn stracciatella over the top and bake for a further 5 minutes until it softens and begins to melt.
Rest for 5 minutes, then scatter the thinly sliced radish over the top and finish with a little black pepper. Serve straight from the dish.

tips: Cook the pasta until still firm, as it will soften further in the oven.
Add the stracciatella late so it stays soft and creamy rather than drying out.
Slice the radish as thinly as you can for the best peppery crunch.

Fold the eel back through the pasta along with the sauerkraut and the remaining black pepper. Taste and add a pinch more salt only if needed.
Divide between two warm bowls. Top with the golden halloumi and scatter over the chopped mixed nuts and raisins for crunch and sweetness. Serve straight away.

tips: Fry the halloumi just before serving, as it is at its best while still hot and squeaky.
Keep the reserved cooking water to hand: its starch helps the butter and kimchi juices cling to the fettuccine.
Chop the nuts just before using so they stay crunchy against the soft pasta.

steps.text: Bring the water to a rolling boil in a large pan and add the salt. Peel and finely grate the fresh turmeric, and bruise the lemongrass along its length with the back of a knife so it releases its scent.

Add the spaghetti to the boiling water and simmer briskly, stirring now and then, until just tender with a little bite. Before draining, scoop out a mugful of the starchy pasta water and set it aside.
While the pasta cooks, heat the cooking oil in a frying pan over a medium-high heat. Fry the halloumi slabs for 1 to 2 minutes each side until deep golden and squeaky. Transfer to a plate.

In a large wide pan over a medium-low heat, melt the butter. Add the grated turmeric and bruised lemongrass and let them sizzle gently for 2 minutes, stirring, until the butter turns golden and fragrant. Take care not to let it brown.

Drain the spaghetti and tip it into the turmeric butter. Add the tahini sauce and a splash of the reserved pasta water, then toss over the heat, adding more water a little at a time, until the sauce is glossy and clings to every strand.
Lift out and discard the lemongrass. Season with black pepper and taste for salt.

Divide the spaghetti between two warm bowls. Top with the halloumi, then scatter over the crumbled onion bhajis for crunch and dot with pieces of Rocamadour. Finish with a pinch of dried mint and a little more black pepper, and serve straight away.

tips: Wear gloves or wash your hands promptly after grating the turmeric, as it stains skin and worktops bright yellow.
Add the bhajis just before serving so they stay crunchy rather than softening in the sauce.
Pat the halloumi very dry before frying for the best golden crust.
